nodes.name: Ru/Ni Impregnation and Pyrolysis
nodes.procedure: Ru and Ni metal salts with varied Ru:Ni ratios (including 3:1 for Ru3Ni-N-C, 5:1 for Ru5Ni-N-C, 1:1 for RuNi-N-C, 1:2 for RuNi2-N-C, pure Ru for Ru-N-C, pure Ni for Ni-N-C) were anchored onto the N–C support via a facile wet-impregnation protocol, followed by subsequent pyrolysis to yield the Ru_x Ni_y–N–C electrocatalysts (where x:y represents the Ru:Ni atomic ratio) and reference materials Ru–N–C and Ni–N–C.
nodes.source_text: Ru and Ni metal salts with varied Ru:Ni ratios were anchored onto the N–C support via a facile wet-impregnation protocol, followed by subsequent pyrolysis to yield the RuNi electrocatalyst (referred to as Ru_x Ni_y –N–C , where x:y represents the Ru : Ni atomic ratio). We also synthesized pure Ru nanoparticles supported on N–C (denoted Ru–N–C) for comparative study.

nodes.name: Ru3Ni–N–C
aliases: R u _ { 3 } N i - N - C

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru₃Ni–N–C exhibits dodecahedral morphology with metal nanoclusters uniformly dispersed on carbon matrix.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Both Ru_x Ni_y –N–C and Ru–N–C electrocatalysts exhibit a dodecahedral morphology with metal nanoclusters uniformly dispersed on the carbon matrix... Fig. 1b, c and Fig. S1–S5, ESI†.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru₃Ni–N–C shows dodecahedral morphology with uniformly dispersed Ru₃Ni alloy nanoclusters on N–C support.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The microscopic morphology of the as-prepared catalysts was investigated using... transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Fig. 1b, c and Fig. S1–S5, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru₃Ni–N–C shows lattice fringes of 0.203 nm and 0.210 nm corresponding to (101) and (100) faces of Ru₃Ni alloy; Ru–N–C shows 0.207 nm for Ru (101) and 0.214 nm for Ru (100).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Closer observation from high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of a representative sample, Ru₃Ni–N–C, indicates two different lattice fringes with lattice spacings of 0.203 nm and 0.210 nm, corresponding to the (101) and (100) faces of the Ru₃Ni alloy, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Coexistence of atomically dispersed Ni single-atoms (yellow circles) with Ru₃Ni alloy nanoclusters (red circles) observed in Ru₃Ni–N–C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Atomic-resolution high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) was performed to investigate the distribution of Ru and Ni species at the atomic scale.

nodes.characterization_summary: Element mapping and line-scan profile confirm Ni single-atoms tightly packed around Ru₃Ni alloy nanoclusters in Ru₃Ni–N–C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Several Ni single-atoms (yellow circles) are tightly packed around an Ru₃Ni alloy nanocluster (red circle), which is further demonstrated by the element mapping images and line-scan profile of the electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) of Ru₃Ni–N–C (Fig. 1f and Fig. S10, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Introduction of Ni positively shifts the main XRD peak at ~44° corresponding to Ru (101) plane, indicating RuNi alloy formation with lattice compressive strain.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The crystal structure was then examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD). As shown in Fig. S6 (ESI†), the introduction of Ni positively shifts the main peak at approximately 44° corresponding to the (101) crystal plane of Ru.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru–N–C shows negligible strain; Ru₃Ni–N–C shows compressive strain along ε_xx and minor shear strain along ε_xy.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The geometric phase analysis (GPA) results further reveal that the Ru–N–C sample exhibits negligible strain components along ε_xx, ε_yy and ε_xy directions... In contrast, Ru₃Ni–N–C demonstrates relatively significant lattice distortion.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru 3p Ru⁰ peak negatively shifts and Ni 2p Ni⁰ peak positively shifts in Ru₃Ni–N–C, indicating electron transfer from Ni to Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was conducted to monitor the surface electronic structure of the catalysts. As displayed in the high-resolution Ru 3p spectra (Fig. S12a, ESI†), the Ru⁰ peak of Ru₃Ni–N–C exhibits a negative shift relative to that of Ru–N–C.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge XANES of Ru₃Ni–N–C approaches Ru-foil (Ru oxidation state +0.86); Ni K-edge shows coexistence of Ni single-atoms (+1.54) and Ru₃Ni alloy.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ru K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectrum reveals that the absorption edge of Ru₃Ni–N–C approaches that of Ru-foil... Ru oxidation states in Ru/C, Ru–N–C and Ru₃Ni–N–C were estimated to be +0.53, +1.18 and +0.86, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge FT-EXAFS shows Ru-Ni(Ru) at 2.67 Å in Ru₃Ni–N–C (shorter than Ru–Ru 2.69 Å); Ni K-edge shows Ni-Ru(Ni) at 2.61 Å and Ni–N at 1.86 Å.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The coordination environments of Ru and Ni in Ru₃Ni–N–C, Ru–N–C and Ni–N–C catalysts were then investigated with the Fourier transforms of extended X-ray absorption fine-structure (FT-EXAFS) spectra.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru₃Ni–N–C exhibits largest electrochemical double layer capacitance C_dl = 41 mF cm⁻², demonstrating maximum ECSA.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Obviously, Ru₃Ni–N–C exhibits the largest C_dl (41 mF cm⁻²), demonstrating maximum utilization of noble metal atoms.

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP-AES used to determine Ru/Pt content for mass activity normalization.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The mass activities (MA) of the catalysts were calculated by normalizing the kinetic current per unit mass Ru or Pt based on the inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES) results (Table S3 and Fig. S16, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru₃Ni–N–C shows lowest charge transfer resistance R_ct = 32.5 Ω.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The accelerated HER kinetics on Ru₃Ni–N–C were also confirmed by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements. The Nyquist plot (Fig. S21, ESI†) reveals that Ru₃Ni–N–C exhibits the smallest semicircle.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman shows interfacial water species (4-HB-H₂O, 2-HB-H₂O, K⁺-H₂O) with Stark slopes 14.2, 25.3, 53.1 cm⁻¹ V⁻¹ respectively; Ru₃Ni–N–C shows strongest water interaction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Given the superior HER activity of Ru₃Ni–N–C in alkaline media, we monitored the water structure on the electrode–electrolyte interface by employing in situ Raman spectroscopy.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-stability TEM shows Ru₃Ni–N–C mean particle size remains 5.03 nm (vs 4.95 nm fresh), confirming structural stability.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The TEM image post-stability testing clearly demonstrates that the mean particle size of the alloy nanoclusters remains at 5.03 nm, which closely matches the value observed in the fresh sample 4.95 nm, Fig. S22, ESI†.
